text: Revised Schedule M was notified as G.S.R. 922(E), New Delhi, 28 Dec 2023 (file F.No. X.11014/2/2017-DRS), using the rule-making powers in sections 12 and 33 of the 1940 Act, after DTAB consultation. It substitutes a new Schedule M in the Drugs Rules 1945 and retitles it to cover GMP plus requirements of premises, plant and equipment; rules 74(o), 76(8) and 78(p) were amended to use the new title. The draft was G.S.R. 999(E) of 5 Oct 2018.

text: As of Sep 2026 revised Schedule M binds every licensed manufacturer in India, large and MSME, from 1 Jan 2026 at the latest. In Nov 2025 CDSCO told state and UT drug controllers to start risk-based Schedule M inspections and report findings monthly; late-Dec 2025 reporting said the ministry would not extend the MSME date again; only about 1,600-1,700 MSME units had filed upgradation plans. text: Revised Schedule M has 13 Parts. Part I holds the main GMP principles in 20 numbered sections: 1 pharmaceutical quality system; 2 quality risk management and product quality review; 3 GMP for pharmaceutical products; 4 sanitation and hygiene; 5 qualification and validation; 6 complaints and adverse reactions; 7 product recalls; 8 change control; 9 loan-licence/contract production and analysis; 10 self-inspection, quality audits, supplier audits; 11 personnel (key personnel, training, hygiene); 12 premises; 13 equipment; 14 materials; 15 reference standards; 16 waste materials; 17 documentation; 18 good practices in production; 19 good practices in quality control; 20 computerised systems. Parts II-XII add product-specific rules that apply on top of Part I (each says Part I applies mutatis mutandis): II sterile products, parenterals (SVP and LVP) and sterile ophthalmics; III hazardous substances (sex hormones, steroids, cytotoxics); IV biologicals; V radiopharmaceuticals; VI phytopharmaceuticals; VII investigational products for clinical trials; VIII oral solid dosage forms (tablets and capsules); IX oral liquids; X topical/external preparations; XI metered-dose inhalers; XII APIs (ICH Q7-style). Part XIII lists recommended plant, equipment and minimum areas per dosage form. The Tablets edition needs Parts I, VIII and XIII (tablets section); the Injectables edition needs Parts I, II and XIII (parenteral sections); Part III applies to either edition when hormones, steroids or cytotoxics are handled.

text: Alignment: Part I follows the structure and much of the wording of WHO GMP main principles (WHO TRS 986 Annex 2, 2014), adding QRM, product quality review, change control and a computerised-systems section. Part XII follows ICH Q7. Part II (sterile) follows WHO/PIC/S-style A-D grading. India is not a PIC/S member; the revision is widely described as moving toward WHO-GMP and PIC/S expectations, not as formal PIC/S equivalence.

clause: Part I, section 1 (PQS), 1.1-1.7 and the PQS 'shall ensure' list
url: https://egazette.gov.in (G.S.R. 922(E)); text checked in user-supplied copy, lines 28-40, 997-1017, 1044-1069
requirement: The manufacturer must run a documented pharmaceutical quality system covering GMP and QRM, with a quality manual, senior-management responsibility and management reviews of the PQS at least once a year unless otherwise justified. Product and process monitoring results must feed into batch release and deviation investigations, and planned changes must be evaluated and approved before implementation and reviewed afterwards.
system_implications: The eBMR is one component of the PQS: it must expose batch outcomes (deviations, yields, IPC trends, release decisions) as data for management review and PQR, and it must link to change control so that an MBR version cannot be activated without an approved change record.
verification_test: Generate a management-review data extract for a 12-month window and confirm it contains per-product deviation counts, yield trends and release/reject counts; try to activate an MBR version with no approved change-control reference and confirm it is blocked.
note: confirmed in official text

clause: Part I, section 1 (PQS), 'shall ensure' item (s); section 3.1 (basic GMP requirements, items 6 and 7)
url: https://egazette.gov.in (G.S.R. 922(E)); text checked in user-supplied copy, lines 252-263, 980, 1087-1089
requirement: Records must be made during manufacture, by hand, by recording instruments or both, showing that every required step was actually done and that quantity and quality are as expected. Significant deviations must be fully recorded and investigated to root cause, with CAPA whose effectiveness is monitored. Manufacturing and distribution records must let the whole history of a batch be traced and must be kept in an understandable, accessible form.
system_implications: Contemporaneous step capture (manual entry or instrument interface) for every MBR step; mandatory deviation capture with root-cause and CAPA links; full forward/backward batch genealogy including distribution; long-term human-readable rendering of the complete record.
verification_test: Execute a test batch, skip a step and confirm the record cannot be completed; raise a deviation and confirm it cannot be closed without a root cause and a CAPA reference; run a genealogy query from a finished-goods batch back to every input lot and forward to distribution records.
note: confirmed in official text

clause: Part I, section 2.3 (product quality review), 2.3.1-2.3.3
url: https://egazette.gov.in (G.S.R. 922(E)); text checked in user-supplied copy, lines 750-935, 977-978, 1040-1042
requirement: Regular, periodic or rolling quality reviews are required for every product, expressly including products made for export only, normally each year. Minimum inputs include starting and packaging materials (especially new sources and API supply-chain traceability), critical in-process and finished-product results, failed batches, significant deviations and CAPA effectiveness, process or method changes, dossier variations, stability results, returns, complaints and recalls, earlier CAPA adequacy, post-marketing commitments, equipment and utility qualification status, and technical agreements. Results must be assessed for CAPA or revalidation; grouping by product type is allowed if justified; the authorised person must ensure the review is timely and accurate.
system_implications: The eBMR must store IPC results, yields, deviations, rejects and material-lot sources as structured, queryable data per product and period, including export-only SKUs, and provide a PQR extract; the PQR record should carry the authorised person's sign-off.
verification_test: Run the PQR extract for a product with a mix of domestic and export-only batches and confirm all batches, IPC statistics, failed batches and linked deviations/CAPA appear; confirm the extract identifies which material suppliers were new in the period.
note: confirmed in official text; EU Chapter 1.10 also covers export-only products and FDA 211.180(e) requires an annual review, so this is equivalent rather than stricter.

clause: Part I, section 2 (QRM)
url: https://egazette.gov.in (G.S.R. 922(E)); text checked in user-supplied copy, lines 944-953, 968-969, 986-987
requirement: There must be a QRM system: a systematic process to assess, control, communicate and review risks to product quality, usable both before and after the fact. Risk evaluation must rest on scientific knowledge and process experience and link to patient protection, and the effort, formality and documentation of QRM must match the level of risk.
system_implications: Risk ratings should be attributes of MBR steps, deviations and change requests (for example to decide which steps need second-person verification or which deviations need full investigation); the system should record the rationale behind risk-based choices.
verification_test: Classify a deviation as minor and confirm the workflow requires a documented risk rationale; change a step's criticality in a new MBR version and confirm verification requirements change accordingly.
note: confirmed in official text

clause: Part I, 11.3.6-11.3.10 (authorised person and batch release) and section 1 PQS 'shall ensure' list item (i)
url: https://egazette.gov.in (G.S.R. 922(E)); text checked in user-supplied copy, lines 144-246, 624-626, 646-649, 997-999
requirement: No batch may be sold or supplied until the authorised person has certified it. The authorised person answers for technical and regulatory compliance and approves release after assessing production conditions, in-process results, the manufacturing and packaging documentation, specification compliance and the finished pack. Before release they must confirm, among other things: licence and product approval conditions met; GMP followed; main processes validated; all checks done with production conditions and records considered; planned changes or deviations reported through a defined system (some may need licensing-authority notification or approval) and covered by extra testing; all production and QC documentation completed and endorsed by trained supervisors; the head of QC has approved; and all relevant factors considered. The release function may be delegated to a qualified designated person under an approved procedure, normally QA through batch review.
system_implications: Release workflow with a configurable 'Authorised Person' role and an optional delegate role, both bound to named, qualified users; hard prerequisites before the release signature: all steps signed, all deviations closed or assessed, head-of-QC approval captured, change/deviation regulatory-notification flag checked; the checklist items should be recorded as part of the release record. For EU-market batches the same slot must be filled by a QP certification; for FDA the quality unit approval.
verification_test: Attempt release with (a) an open deviation, (b) missing head-of-QC approval, (c) an unsigned step, and (d) a user lacking the AP or delegate role; each must be blocked. Release with a delegate and confirm the record shows the delegation basis (procedure reference).
note: confirmed in official text. India uses an 'authorised person' plus explicit head-of-QC approval rather than an EU QP or the FDA quality unit; the WHO-derived checklist is similar to EU Annex 16 but the legal role differs. Clause reference corrected: the 'no sale before certification' item sits in the section 1 PQS list, not in 3.1.

url: https://egazette.gov.in (G.S.R. 922(E)); text checked in user-supplied copy, lines 98-99, 375-381, 451-455, 618
requirement: Key personnel are the head(s) of production, the head(s) of the quality units (QA and QC, which may be combined) and the authorised person, normally full-time. Heads of production and quality must be independent of each other; tasks may be delegated but not responsibility. The production head must ensure a designated person reviews and signs the production records; the quality heads evaluate batch records and approve or reject materials and products.
system_implications: Role model must separate production-head, QA-head, QC-head and authorised-person roles and prevent one user from holding both production-head and quality-head approval rights on the same batch (segregation of duties); a 'production record reviewer' signature distinct from the QA review signature.
verification_test: Assign one user both production-head and QA-head roles and confirm the system refuses or flags the conflict; confirm a batch cannot reach QA review until the designated production reviewer has signed.
note: confirmed in official text

clause: Part I, 17.2 (general documentation clauses; retention sentence probably 17.2.7)
url: https://egazette.gov.in (G.S.R. 922(E)); text checked in user-supplied copy, lines 2020-2022
requirement: Records must be made or completed at the time each action is taken so that all significant manufacturing activities are traceable, and they must be kept until at least one year has passed since the finished product expired.
system_implications: Retention engine: India rule = batch expiry date + 1 year. EU Chapter 4 requires the longer of expiry + 1 year or 5 years after QP certification, so exported-to-EU batches need the EU rule; FDA 211.180 is expiry + 1 year (or 3 years after distribution for some exempt OTC products). Compute the retention date per batch as the maximum over the batch's target markets and block deletion or archiving before it.
verification_test: Create batches with 24-month shelf life for India-only and for India+EU; confirm computed retention dates are expiry+1y (about 3 years after manufacture) and max(expiry+1y, certification+5y) respectively, and that purge is refused before those dates.
note: confirmed in official text. Clause number inferred from WHO ordering because the page is scrambled. India is equal to FDA and less strict than EU here; also check Drugs Rules conditions of licence for any separate period (see open questions).

clause: Part I, 17.2 (general documentation clauses: approval, review, entries, alterations)
url: https://egazette.gov.in (G.S.R. 922(E)); text checked in user-supplied copy, lines 2053-2065, 2100-2103, 2141-2142, 2154-2155
requirement: Documents need careful design, drafting, review and distribution, must match the licence, be approved, signed and dated by responsible persons, and not be changed without authorisation. They must be clear, orderly and easy to check; copies made from master documents must not introduce errors. Documents are reviewed regularly; a system must stop use of superseded versions, which are kept for a defined period. Data entries must be clear, legible and indelible with enough space. Any alteration must be signed and dated, leave the original readable and, where appropriate, give the reason.
system_implications: MBR and SOP document control with approval signatures, effective dates and automatic withdrawal of superseded versions from execution; superseded versions archived for a configured period; every correction to a recorded value keeps the old value visible in the record and audit trail, with signer, timestamp and a reason (make the reason mandatory to satisfy FDA/EU data-integrity expectations as well).
verification_test: Supersede an MBR version and confirm new batches cannot be started from it while the old version remains retrievable; correct a recorded weight and confirm the rendered BMR shows original value, new value, who, when and why.
note: confirmed in official text (WHO-derived wording; reason for change is 'where appropriate', same as EU Chapter 4.9).

clause: Part I, 17.2 (electronic data-processing clause; probably 17.2.8)
url: https://egazette.gov.in (G.S.R. 922(E)); text checked in user-supplied copy, lines 2004-2013
requirement: Data and records may be held electronically, photographically or by another dependable method, provided the master formulae and detailed SOPs for the system are available and record accuracy is checked. With electronic handling, only authorised persons may enter or change data, changes and deletions must be recorded, access must be limited by passwords or similar, and critical data entry must be independently checked. Electronically stored batch records must be protected by backup (tape, microfilm, discs, paper printouts or other means) and stay readily available throughout retention.
system_implications: Explicit legal basis for an eBMR under Schedule M. Needs role-based access, an audit trail of changes and deletions, second-person or system verification of critical entries, validated backup and restore, and readable retrieval for the full retention period.
verification_test: Log in as a user without edit rights and confirm edits are refused; change and delete a value and confirm both appear in the audit trail; restore a backup to a test instance and confirm a closed batch record renders completely.
note: confirmed in official text (WHO TRS 986 wording).

clause: Part I, section 20 (computerised systems), 20.2-20.10 (20.1 heading text lost in extraction; the Part XII twin 5.4.1 requires validation scaled to diversity, complexity and criticality)
url: https://egazette.gov.in (G.S.R. 922(E)); text checked in user-supplied copy, lines 2336-2374, 3280, 3311-3318; Part XII 5.4.1 at line 6918
requirement: Computerised systems must be shown fit for their tasks by installation and operational qualification; qualified commercial software needs less testing, and an unvalidated legacy system may be validated retrospectively if documentation exists. Systems must stop unauthorised access or data changes, prevent missing data (for example data not captured while the system was off) and record each data change with the previous value, who changed it and when. Written procedures must cover operation and maintenance. Manual entry of critical data needs an extra accuracy check by a second person or by the system. Incidents that could affect product quality or record reliability must be recorded and investigated. System changes go through change control, formally authorised, documented and tested, with records showing a validated state. A backup must prevent permanent record loss, with data protection for all systems, and a secondary (non-computer) record of the data is permitted as well.
system_implications: eBMR must ship with a validation package (URS, risk assessment, IQ/OQ, traceability) usable by Indian customers; audit trail with old value, new value, user and timestamp; completeness controls (heartbeat or sequence checks so that equipment data gaps are detected and flagged); second-person or system verification for critical manual entries; incident log for system failures linked to affected batches; configuration change control; backup/restore; option to capture a parallel paper or secondary record.
verification_test: Stop an equipment data feed mid-step and confirm the gap is flagged in the batch record; enter a critical value manually and confirm a verifier signature or system check is required; apply a configuration change without an approved change record and confirm it is refused; verify audit entries show the previous value.
note: confirmed in official text for 20.2-20.10. No Part I clause requires audit-trail review or gives detailed e-signature rules; those come from FDA Part 11 / EU Annex 11 and should be applied for all markets.

clause: Part I, 17.3.6 (master formula records), 17.3.6.1-17.3.6.2
url: https://egazette.gov.in (G.S.R. 922(E)); text checked in user-supplied copy, lines 1222-1272
requirement: A formally authorised master formula must exist for each product and each batch size. It must cover: product name with a product reference code linked to its specification; dosage form, strength and batch size; all starting materials (with INNs where applicable) with amounts, designated name and unique material reference, noting any substance lost during processing; expected final yield with limits and relevant intermediate yields; processing location and principal equipment; methods (or references) for preparing and operating critical equipment such as cleaning, assembly, calibration, sterilisation and use; detailed stepwise instructions (material checks, pre-treatments, order of addition, mixing times, temperatures); in-process controls with limits; storage requirements including container, labelling and special conditions; special precautions; and the permitted hold time for intermediate and in-process material.
system_implications: MBR data model: one approved master per product + batch size (or scaled masters, each approved); mandatory fields for product code, spec reference, INN, 'lost in processing' flag (e.g., granulation water or solvents), yield limits per stage, equipment class and room, IPC limits and hold times per intermediate. MBR approval must fail validation if any mandatory element, especially hold time, is empty.
verification_test: Try to approve an MBR without hold times or without yield limits and confirm validation errors; approve an MBR for 100 kg and confirm a 200 kg batch cannot be issued from it without its own approved master.
note: confirmed in official text. The hold-time element is an Indian addition to the WHO list (FDA 211.111 only requires time limits where appropriate; EU 4.17 does not list hold time). 'Each batch size' matches WHO and EU wording.

clause: Part I, 17.3.7 (packaging instructions)
url: https://egazette.gov.in (G.S.R. 922(E)); text checked in user-supplied copy, lines 1274-1293, 1995
requirement: Formally authorised packaging instructions are needed for each product, pack size and pack type. They normally cover: product name; dosage form, strength and (where relevant) method of application; pack size by count, weight or volume; a complete list of packaging materials for a standard batch with quantities, sizes, types and each material's specification code; where appropriate a specimen of the printed packaging material showing where batch number and expiry date go; special precautions including line-clearance checks of the area and equipment before and after packaging; a description of the operation, subsidiary operations and equipment; and in-process controls with sampling instructions and acceptance limits.
system_implications: Master packaging record (MPR) is a separate approved object per product x pack size x pack type, linked to the MBR; it stores a packaging bill of materials with spec codes and an image of each approved artwork with the coding positions marked; line-clearance checklists before and after; IPC definitions with sampling plan and limits.
verification_test: Create two pack sizes for one product and confirm each needs its own approved MPR; confirm a packaging order cannot start unless the MPR has artwork specimens attached for every printed component.
note: confirmed in official text (matches WHO 15.23 and EU 4.19).

clause: Part I, 17.3.8 (batch processing records), 17.3.8.1-17.3.8.3
url: https://egazette.gov.in (G.S.R. 922(E)); text checked in user-supplied copy, lines 1295-1328, 2017-2033, 2040-2043, 2067-2071
requirement: A batch processing record is kept for every batch, built from the currently approved documents, prepared so as to avoid errors (copying or validated computer programs are recommended; transcription from approved documents is to be avoided). Before processing, a recorded check confirms that equipment and workstation are free of previous products, documents and materials and that equipment is clean and suitable. During processing each item is recorded when the action is taken, and on completion the record is dated and signed by the person responsible for processing. Items: product name; batch number; dates and times of starting significant intermediate stages and of completing production; name of the person responsible for each stage; initials of operators of significant steps and, where appropriate, of checkers (e.g., weighing); batch or analytical control number and actual quantity of each starting material weighed, including any recovered or reprocessed material added; relevant operations, events and major equipment; permitted hold time for intermediate and in-process material; IPCs with performer initials and results; yields at pertinent stages with explanations of significant deviations from expected yield; notes on special problems with signed authorisation for any departure from the master formula.
system_implications: This is the core eBMR content model. Generate the batch record electronically from the approved MBR (no re-typing); capture timestamps at stage start and batch completion; person-responsible per stage plus performer and verifier identities per step; lot/AR number and actual weight per material including recovered material flag; equipment IDs; hold-time start/stop with limit check; IPC results with performer; stage yields with mandatory comment when outside limits; deviation notes with authorisation signature; final signature of the person responsible for processing.
verification_test: Execute a batch end-to-end and confirm the rendered record contains every listed item; enter an out-of-limit stage yield and confirm a comment and deviation link are forced; exceed a hold time and confirm the system blocks or raises a deviation; confirm the completed record carries the dated signature of the processing-responsible person.
note: confirmed in official text. Mostly equal to WHO/EU 4.20 and FDA 211.188; the hold-time item and the 'person responsible for each stage' are explicit Indian additions.

clause: Part I, 17.3.9 (batch packaging records), 17.3.9.1-17.3.9.3
url: https://egazette.gov.in (G.S.R. 922(E)); text checked in user-supplied copy, lines 1345-1372, 1839, 1871, 1879, 1891-1894, 1912-1914, 1929-1932, 1962-1966
requirement: A batch packaging record is kept for each batch or part-batch packed, based on the approved packaging instructions and prepared to avoid errors (copying or validated computer programs recommended). Before packaging, a recorded check confirms equipment and workstation are clear of previous products, documents and materials and are clean and suitable. Each item is recorded when the action happens, with date and responsible person identified by signature or electronic password: product name, batch number and bulk quantity to be packed, finished-product batch number, planned and actual quantity and the reconciliation; date and time of packaging operations; name of the responsible person; initials of operators of significant steps; identity and conformity checks against the instructions including IPC results; details of operations, equipment and lines, plus instructions or records for unpacked product returned to store; where possible, samples of printed packaging materials used, including specimens showing print approval and periodic checks of batch number, expiry date and overprinting; notes on special problems and deviations with written authorisation; and quantities and reference numbers of all printed materials and bulk issued, used, destroyed or returned, and product obtained, allowing a proper reconciliation.
system_implications: Separate eBPR per packaging batch or part-batch linked to the bulk batch; electronic identification of the signer is expressly acceptable ('electronic password'); scanned or photographed specimens of printed materials (carton, label, foil) with the coded batch/expiry/MRP overprint captured at start and at intervals; component issue/use/destroy/return ledger with automatic reconciliation.
verification_test: Run a packaging order with two part-batches and confirm two linked packaging records; attach coding specimens at start, mid-run and end; enter issue/used/destroyed/returned quantities that do not balance and confirm the record cannot close without an investigation reference.
note: confirmed in official text (matches WHO 15.26 and EU 4.21 closely; 'signature or electronic password' wording is WHO's).

clause: Part I, 17.3.10.8-17.3.10.11 (batch numbering)
url: https://egazette.gov.in (G.S.R. 922(E)); text checked in user-supplied copy, lines 1570-1584
requirement: An SOP must define the batch (lot) numbering system so each intermediate, bulk and finished batch has its own number; processing and packaging numbering must be related; numbers must never be reused, including for reprocessing; each allocation must be recorded at once (e.g., in a logbook) with at least the allocation date, product identity and batch size.
system_implications: Configurable batch-number generator with a global uniqueness constraint per site (never recycled, even after cancellation), a rule linking bulk and packaging batch numbers, and an allocation register storing date, product and batch size.
verification_test: Cancel a batch and confirm its number is never reissued; attempt manual entry of an existing number and confirm rejection; export the allocation register and confirm the three required fields.
note: confirmed in official text

clause: Part I, 18.2.2 (deviations) and 18.5.12 (batch record review and failure investigation)
url: https://egazette.gov.in (G.S.R. 922(E)); text checked in user-supplied copy, lines 1541-1544, 1767-1772
requirement: Departures from instructions or procedures should be avoided; where they happen they must follow an approved procedure and be authorised in writing by a designated person, with QC involvement where appropriate. Production records must be reviewed as part of batch-release approval before going to the authorised person. Any divergence or specification failure must be investigated thoroughly, extended where needed to other batches and products, and written up with conclusion and follow-up.
system_implications: Deviation workflow: capture at point of occurrence, authorisation e-signature by a designated role (optionally with QC co-approval), impact assessment that can list other affected batches/products, conclusion and follow-up actions; production review step as a mandatory state before AP review.
verification_test: Raise a deviation and confirm it needs designated-person approval before the step can continue; confirm the batch cannot move to AP review until production review is signed; add linked batches to an investigation and confirm they are flagged.
note: confirmed in official text

clause: Part I, 18.2.3, 18.4.6 and 18.5.10 (yields and reconciliation)
url: https://egazette.gov.in (G.S.R. 922(E)); text checked in user-supplied copy, lines 1548-1549, 1448, 1760-1762
requirement: Yield checks and reconciliation of quantities must be done as needed to show no discrepancy outside acceptable limits. Any significant deviation from expected yield must be recorded and investigated. Any significant or unusual discrepancy found when reconciling bulk, printed packaging materials and units produced must be investigated, explained and recorded before release.
system_implications: Automatic yield calculation at each stage against MBR limits; automatic reconciliation of printed components and bulk; out-of-limit results open a deviation that blocks release until closed.
verification_test: Enter a stage yield below the lower limit and a carton reconciliation with a 2% unexplained loss (above configured limit); confirm deviations open automatically and release is blocked.
note: confirmed in official text

clause: Part I, 18.2.5, 18.4.1-18.4.2, 18.5.2-18.5.3 (identification and line clearance)
url: https://egazette.gov.in (G.S.R. 922(E)); text checked in user-supplied copy, lines 1556-1563, 1415-1426, 1828-1829, 1853-1857
requirement: Throughout processing, materials, bulk containers, major equipment and, where appropriate, rooms and packaging lines must show the product, strength and batch number, and the stage where applicable; recording the previous product can help. Before any processing or packaging, the area, lines, printers and equipment must be checked clean and free of earlier products, materials, labels and documents; packaging line clearance follows a procedure and checklist and is recorded. Needed in-process and environmental controls must be done and recorded. Each packaging station or line must display the product name and batch number.
system_implications: Room/line/equipment status model (in use by product X batch Y, cleaned, to be cleaned) with printable or on-screen status labels; electronic line-clearance checklist as a gating step before and after each operation, recording the previous product; environmental readings captured into the batch record.
verification_test: Try to start compression or packaging on a line whose status is 'to be cleaned' and confirm it is blocked; complete line clearance and confirm the checklist, signer, time and previous product appear in the batch record.
note: confirmed in official text

clause: Part I, 18.5.4-18.5.11 (packaging operations)
url: https://egazette.gov.in (G.S.R. 922(E)); text checked in user-supplied copy, lines 1385-1403, 1412-1413, 1699-1707, 1755-1766, 1781-1784
requirement: Labelling should follow filling and sealing quickly, or controls must prevent mix-ups. Any printing of codes or expiry dates, on-line or separate, must be checked and recorded, and hand printing re-checked at intervals. Extra care is needed with cut labels, off-line overprinting and hand packing; electronic code readers, label counters and similar devices must be checked for correct operation, and manual labelling needs more frequent checks. Printed or embossed information must be distinct and fade-resistant. On-line checks must at least cover pack appearance, completeness, correct product and materials, correct overprint and working line monitors; samples taken off the line are not returned. Product from an unusual event goes back only after inspection, investigation and approval, with a detailed record. After packaging, unused batch-coded materials are destroyed with a record; uncoded printed materials go back to stock only after documented checks.
system_implications: Packaging IPC schedule with configurable frequency (tighter for manual labelling); challenge-test records for vision systems, barcode/2D-code readers and counters at start, intervals and end; coding verification entries; 'unusual event' sub-workflow; destruction record for coded leftovers; controlled return-to-stock for uncoded items.
verification_test: Configure a start-of-run camera/reader challenge and confirm packaging cannot begin until it passes; record a reader failure mid-run and confirm product since the last good challenge is placed on hold; close the order with coded cartons outstanding and confirm a destruction entry is required.
note: confirmed in official text

clause: Part I, 14.14, 14.16-14.20 (dispensing and use of starting materials)
url: https://egazette.gov.in (G.S.R. 922(E)); text checked in user-supplied copy, lines 1191-1198, 2096-2098, 2112, 2282-2283
requirement: Only starting materials released by QC and within shelf life may be used. There must be means of confirming the identity of the contents of every container, and sampled bulk containers must be identified. Dispensing is done only by designated persons under a written procedure, into clean, properly labelled containers, with accurate weighing or measuring. Each dispensed material and its weight or volume must be independently checked and recorded. Materials dispensed for a batch are kept together and clearly labelled as such.
system_implications: Dispensing module: container-level barcode identity check; hard block on status other than 'released' and on expired or past-retest lots; role check for designated dispensers; second-person verification or validated balance interface for every weighing; dispensed-kit labels linking to the batch.
verification_test: Scan a quarantined lot, an expired lot and a lot past retest date and confirm all are refused; weigh without a verifier and confirm the step cannot be signed unless the balance is a validated interface configured as the independent check.
note: confirmed in official text (FDA 211.101(c)-(d) has an equivalent second-person or automated check).

clause: Part I, 14.32-14.34 (reworking, recovery, reprocessing)
url: https://egazette.gov.in (G.S.R. 922(E)); text checked in user-supplied copy, lines 1188-1189, 2091-2094, 2107-2110
requirement: Reworking or recovering rejected product must be exceptional, allowed only if final quality is unaffected and specifications are met, and done under a defined, authorised procedure after risk evaluation; a record is kept and the reworked batch gets a new batch number. Blending some or all of an earlier in-specification batch into a later batch of that product, at a set process stage, needs prior authorisation, follow a defined procedure after risk evaluation (including shelf-life impact) and be recorded. QC must consider extra testing of any finished product that was reprocessed, reworked or contains recovered product.
system_implications: Rework is modelled as a new batch with a new number and parent-child genealogy to the rejected batch(es), a rework MBR or approved protocol, and a risk assessment reference; recovered-material additions are pre-authorised steps that record source batch numbers and quantities and feed the shelf-life/expiry assignment logic; QC flag for additional testing.
verification_test: Rework a rejected batch and confirm the system forces a new batch number, links genealogy to the parent, and requires an approved rework procedure and risk assessment; add recovered material without pre-authorisation and confirm the step is blocked.
note: confirmed in official text. The mandatory new batch number for a reworked batch comes from WHO; neither 21 CFR 211.115 nor EU Chapter 5 (5.62-5.64) requires a new number, so this is the stricter rule for Indian products.

clause: Part I, 14.15 (release of non-API raw materials without batch testing)
url: https://egazette.gov.in (G.S.R. 922(E)); text checked in user-supplied copy, lines 1184-1186
requirement: QC may release raw materials other than APIs for manufacturing without specific batch testing, but only on the basis of vendor approval and statistical analysis of earlier test results for that material.
system_implications: Material status engine must support a 'released on vendor history' route for non-API excipients with the statistical justification stored. Because FDA 211.84(d) requires at least an identity test per lot and EU Chapter 5 expects identity testing of every batch/container, a per-market rule must force an identity test for lots destined for FDA/EU-market batches, and the dispensing check must block such lots from those batches.
verification_test: Release an excipient lot without testing under the vendor-history rule, then try to dispense it into a batch whose target markets include the US or EU; confirm the system blocks it until an identity result exists.
note: confirmed in official text. This is a relaxation compared with FDA/EU, so the stricter foreign rule must win for exported products.

clause: Part I, 14.13 (labelling of starting materials) and 14.10-14.12, 14.23-14.25 (receipt and packaging materials)
url: https://egazette.gov.in (G.S.R. 922(E)); text checked in user-supplied copy, lines 1169-1177, 1182, 2125-2127, 2176, 2193-2194, 2258-2262
requirement: Stored starting-material labels must show at least the designated name and internal code, the supplier's batch number and the manufacturer's own control or batch number, the current status (for example quarantined, under test, approved, rejected, returned, recalled) and, where appropriate, an expiry or retest date; with fully validated computerised storage systems, not all of this needs to be human-readable on the label. Each batch within a delivery is treated separately for sampling, testing and release. Every lot or delivery of primary and printed packaging gets a unique reference, and packaging materials are checked on delivery to the packaging area for quantity, identity and conformity with the instructions.
system_implications: If the eBMR or its warehouse module is validated, labels may carry only a barcode or 2D code plus minimal text, with status held in the system; the system is then the authority for material status, so status changes must be audit-trailed and e-signed.
verification_test: Print a barcode-only label for a released lot, scan it at dispensing and confirm name, lot, status and retest date are shown from the system; change status to rejected and confirm the next scan blocks use.
note: confirmed in official text

clause: Part I, 17.3.1 (labels of finished drugs, reference standards and containers)
requirement: Every finished drug must be labelled with at least: drug name; active ingredients (with INNs) and amount of each, plus net contents; the manufacturer's batch number; expiry date and date of manufacture in uncoded form; any special storage or handling conditions; directions for use, warnings and precautions; and the name and address of whoever made it or is responsible for marketing it. Labels on containers, equipment or premises must be clear, unambiguous and in the company's format, optionally colour-coded for status.
system_implications: The packaging record must capture and verify, per pack level, the printed batch number, date of manufacture and expiry date in plain (uncoded) form. Date of manufacture is mandatory on Indian labels (WHO only requires expiry), so artwork templates for India need a Mfg. date field that is optional for EU/US-only packs.
verification_test: Load an India artwork template lacking a manufacturing-date field and confirm MPR approval fails; confirm coding verification in the eBPR checks both manufacturing and expiry dates against batch data.
note: confirmed in official text. Adding 'date of manufacture' to the WHO list is an Indian change; Rule 96 of the Drugs Rules separately requires it on the label.

clause: Part II (sterile products), 4.1-4.6 and Table 1 (clean-area grades and particle limits)
requirement: Sterile manufacture uses four grades (A-D) classified to ISO standards. Table 1 sets maximum particles per cubic metre, at rest and in operation, for sizes of 0.5 and 5.0 micrometres. Grade A: 3,520 and 20 in both states. Grade B: 3,520 and 29 at rest; 352,000 and 2,900 in operation. Grade C: 352,000 and 2,900 at rest; 3,520,000 and 29,000 in operation. Grade D: 3,520,000 and 29,000 at rest; not defined in operation. Grade A unidirectional air must run at about 0.36-0.54 m/s (guidance) measured 15-30 cm below the terminal filter, never below 0.36 m/s at working level, shown by airflow visualisation. Classification is kept separate from routine monitoring.
system_implications: Room and zone master data carry a grade and the limit table; EM results imported into the batch record are checked against grade limits. Because EU Annex 1 (2022) uses different values (e.g., 5.0 micrometre limits at Grade A 'not specified' but trended; Grade C/D 2,930/29,300), the limit table must be market-configurable, and for EU-market batches the EU 2022 values and rules apply.
verification_test: Load Indian and EU limit sets; import a Grade B in-operation 5.0 micrometre count of 3,000/m3 and confirm it exceeds the Indian limit (2,900) and is evaluated under the EU set (2,930) for an EU batch; confirm grade A velocity readings below 0.36 m/s are flagged.
note: confirmed in official text (table values reassembled from scattered cells; they match the WHO TRS 961 Annex 6 / pre-2022 EU Annex 1 table). The minimum working-level velocity sentence appears to be an Indian addition.

clause: Part II, 4.7-4.10 and Table 3 (environmental monitoring; microbial limits)
url: https://egazette.gov.in (G.S.R. 922(E)); text checked in user-supplied copy, lines 2479-2511, 2531-2591, 3032-3034, 3048-3050, 3345-3351
requirement: Clean rooms must be monitored in operation at risk-based locations. Grade A needs particle monitoring for the whole of critical processing, including equipment assembly (with stated exceptions), capturing interventions and transient events and alarming on alert-limit excursions; Grade B uses a similar system at lower frequency. Recovery ('clean-up') after operations of about 15-20 minutes to the at-rest limits. Microbial monitoring (settle plates, active air, contact plates, swabs, glove prints) must be frequent during aseptic work, and monitoring results must be considered when reviewing batch documentation for release. Recommended in-operation microbial limits (average values): Grade A under 1 CFU for air per m3, 4-hour settle plate, contact plate and 5-finger glove print; Grade B 10, 5, 5, 5; Grade C 100, 50, 25; Grade D 200, 100, 50. Alert and action limits must be set; exceeding action limits or an adverse alert trend triggers investigation and CAPA per SOP.
system_implications: The injectables batch record must pull or link EM data (non-viable continuous Grade A counts, viable results by location and session) for the batch's processing window and show excursions to the reviewer; release must be blocked until EM results for the filling window are complete and reviewed. Limits must be configurable per market because EU Annex 1 (2022) requires 'no growth' at Grade A, where any growth needs investigation.
verification_test: Record a Grade A settle plate of 1 CFU during a fill: under the Indian table it breaches '<1' and under the EU set it breaches 'no growth'; confirm both raise an excursion linked to the batch and that release is blocked until the investigation is closed. Confirm release is blocked while any viable plate from the filling window is still incubating.
note: confirmed in official text; table cells reassembled from scattered lines. EU 2022 Annex 1 is stricter on Grade A viable results and on contamination control strategy.

clause: Part II, 5.3-5.7 (process simulation / media fills) and 4.11 (hold times and fill duration)
url: https://egazette.gov.in (G.S.R. 922(E)); text checked in user-supplied copy, lines 2596-2600, 2832-2901
requirement: Aseptic processing must be validated by media fills: three consecutive successful runs initially, repeated at defined intervals and after significant HVAC, equipment or process changes, simulating routine steps, normal and worst-case interventions and each shift and shift change. Container numbers must allow valid evaluation and, for small batches, at least equal the batch size. Target is zero growth; acceptance: under 5,000 units no contaminated unit; 5,000-10,000 units one contaminated unit means investigation and possible repeat, two means revalidation after investigation; over 10,000 units one means investigation, two means revalidation. Intermittent contamination at any size must be investigated, and gross failures must consider impact on batches made since the last good media fill. Media fills are also used to set processing hold times and the maximum fill duration.
system_implications: The eBMR must record, per aseptic batch, which line and qualified media-fill envelope it ran within (fill duration, hold times, interventions performed, operators and shifts), and block or flag batches whose duration, interventions or personnel fall outside the last successful media fill. A media-fill failure must be able to query all batches since the last passing run. Acceptance must be market-configurable: EU Annex 1 (2022) treats any contaminated unit as a failed simulation.
verification_test: Run a batch with fill duration longer than the qualified maximum and confirm a deviation; record an intervention type not simulated in the media fill and confirm it is flagged; mark a media fill failed and confirm the system lists all batches filled on that line since the previous successful run.
note: confirmed in official text. Indian acceptance matches FDA 2004 aseptic guidance and WHO 2011, but is less strict than EU Annex 1 (2022); requalification frequency is only 'defined intervals' (EU and FDA expect about every six months per line/shift).

clause: Part II, 5.12-5.17 (processing time limits, bioburden, endotoxins) and 2.4
url: https://egazette.gov.in (G.S.R. 922(E)); text checked in user-supplied copy, lines 2811-2830, 3284-3288
requirement: The processing stage of cleaned components, bulk containers and equipment must be identified. The intervals from washing/drying to sterilisation and from sterilisation to use must be as short as possible and within validated time limits. The time from starting solution preparation to sterilisation or sterile filtration must be as short as possible, with a maximum permitted time set for each product. Purge or blanket gases must pass a sterilising filter. Bioburden must be tested before sterilisation on every batch for both aseptic and terminally sterilised products (scheduled intervals allowed only for overkill cycles; each batch as an IPC for parametric release), against working limits; endotoxins monitored where appropriate. WFI, relevant intermediates and finished injectables must be monitored for endotoxins by a validated pharmacopoeial method; for LVPs, water or intermediate monitoring is always required.
system_implications: Timers in the injectables MBR: wash-to-sterilise, sterilise-to-use and preparation-start-to-filtration, each with product-specific maximums and hard alarms; a mandatory pre-sterilisation bioburden sample step per batch with result entry and limit check; endotoxin test steps; component/equipment status identification by processing stage.
verification_test: Let the preparation-to-filtration timer exceed the product maximum and confirm a deviation is forced; try to close the batch without a bioburden result and confirm it is blocked; for an LVP product confirm an endotoxin step on water or intermediate cannot be removed from the MBR.
note: confirmed in official text (WHO 2011-derived; EU 2022 and FDA have equivalent expectations).

clause: Part II, 6.5-6.11 (sterilisation: validation, loading, records)
url: https://egazette.gov.in (G.S.R. 922(E)); text checked in user-supplied copy, lines 3359-3421, 2628-2719
requirement: All sterilisation processes must be validated, with effectiveness in every part of each load type shown by physical measurements and, where appropriate, biological indicators, and re-verified at least once a year and after significant equipment changes. Validated loading patterns are required. Every carrier (basket, tray) must be labelled with material name, batch number and sterilised/not-sterilised status. A sterilisation record must exist for every run and be approved as part of batch release. Heat cycles are recorded on suitably accurate equipment with the probe at the validated coolest point, preferably checked against an independent second probe; temperature and pressure both monitored; control instruments independent of monitoring; automated control/monitoring validated; system and cycle faults registered by the system and seen by the operator; vacuum-phase chambers leak-tested regularly. For EO, each cycle records time, pressure, temperature, humidity and gas concentration with a continuous pressure/temperature chart and biological indicators; radiation dose is measured by dosimeters; these records form part of the batch record. Cooling fluids contacting product must be sterile.
system_implications: Steriliser/autoclave/depyrogenation tunnel integration: import each cycle report (cycle ID, load pattern ID, recorder trace, min/max temperature at coolest probe, pressure, F0 where used, alarms) into the batch record; mandatory reviewer sign-off of each cycle before batch release; validated load pattern chosen from a list; annual requalification date checked before the steriliser can be selected; carrier labels printed with batch and status.
verification_test: Select a steriliser whose annual requalification has lapsed and confirm it is blocked; import a cycle report with an alarm and confirm the batch cannot be released until the cycle is reviewed and the alarm dispositioned; confirm the release checklist lists every sterilisation cycle used by the batch.
note: confirmed in official text. 'At least annually' revalidation matches EU Annex 1 expectations; FDA also expects periodic requalification.

clause: Part II, 6.11.2 (aseptic processing and sterile filtration)
url: https://egazette.gov.in (G.S.R. 922(E)); text checked in user-supplied copy, lines 2720-2802
requirement: Aseptic processing must control environment, personnel, critical surfaces, container/closure sterilisation and transfer, the maximum holding time of product before filling, and the sterilising filter. Solutions that cannot be terminally sterilised may be filtered through a 0.22 micrometre (or equivalent) sterile filter into sterilised containers; filtration alone is not enough when terminal sterilisation is possible. A second (redundant) filtration just before filling may be advisable; the final filter should be as close to the fill point as possible; filters must not shed fibres (asbestos filters banned). Filter integrity must be checked before use and confirmed immediately after use (bubble point, diffusion or pressure hold); filtration time for a known volume and the pressure difference are set during validation, with significant routine differences noted and investigated, and the results go into the batch record. Critical vent filters are confirmed after use. A filter may be used for at most one working day unless longer use has been validated.
system_implications: Filtration step template: filter ID/lot, pre-use and post-use integrity results (with instrument printout or data import), filtration start/stop time and differential pressure compared with validated ranges, vent filter post-use test, filter-use duration check against 'one working day'. Hold-time timer from end of compounding to end of filling.
verification_test: Enter a failing post-use integrity result and confirm the batch is put on hold and a deviation opens; reuse a filter ID on a second day without a validated extended-use flag and confirm it is blocked; enter a filtration time outside the validated range and confirm the system requires an investigation note.
note: confirmed in official text. EU Annex 1 (2022) additionally requires pre-use post-sterilisation integrity testing (PUPSIT) unless justified by risk assessment; apply that for EU-market products.

clause: Part II, 2.1-2.3 (sterility testing and release) and 4.8
url: https://egazette.gov.in (G.S.R. 922(E)); text checked in user-supplied copy, lines 2433-2435, 3067-3072, 3086-3087, 3101-3102, 3120-3121, 2534-2535
requirement: The sterility test is only the last of a series of controls and must be validated for the product using pharmacopoeial methods. Sterility samples must represent the whole batch and include the riskiest parts: for aseptic fills, units filled first, last and right after any major stoppage; for heat-sterilised products, the potentially coolest part of the load. Batch processing records, and for aseptic processing the environmental records, must be examined together with sterility results. Parametric release, where authorised, needs special attention to validation and monitoring of the whole process.
system_implications: The batch record must mark sterility sample pull points (start, end, after each significant interruption, coolest load position) and record which units were pulled; the release review screen must present processing record, EM data and sterility result together; a parametric-release mode only if the product licence permits it.
verification_test: Log a significant interruption during filling and confirm the system adds a mandatory sterility sample pull after restart; confirm release review cannot be signed unless the sterility result, EM summary and processing record have each been opened and acknowledged.
note: confirmed in official text

clause: Part II, 10.3-10.8 (finishing: capping, vacuum-sealed containers, inspection) and Part I 11.5.1
url: https://egazette.gov.in (G.S.R. 922(E)); text checked in user-supplied copy, lines 3436-3444, 4170-4175, 4187-4188, 181-182
requirement: Cap crimping generates particles and needs a separate station with extraction; if capping is done outside the aseptic core, vials must stay under Grade A air until crimped; vials with missing or displaced stoppers are rejected before capping, and human intervention at capping must avoid direct contact. Vacuum-sealed containers must be tested for maintained vacuum after a set period. Every filled parenteral container must be inspected individually for extraneous contamination or defects; visual inspection needs controlled lighting and background, inspectors must pass regular eyesight checks (with their own corrective lenses) and get frequent breaks; automated inspection must be validated and its performance checked at intervals; results must be recorded. Staff doing visual inspection must also have periodic eye checks under Part I.
system_implications: 100% inspection step recording inspector identity, booth/lighting check, start/stop times (break enforcement), quantities inspected and rejects by defect category; inspector qualification (eye test and inspection qualification) checked against personnel records before sign-on; automated inspection machine challenge-set results at intervals; stopper-presence reject counts before capping; vacuum-hold test results for vacuum-sealed packs.
verification_test: Assign an inspector whose eyesight check has expired and confirm sign-on is refused; run manual inspection beyond the configured continuous-inspection time and confirm a break prompt/hold; skip an interval challenge on the automated inspection machine and confirm the lot is flagged.
note: confirmed in official text; equivalent to EU Annex 1 (2022) 8.30-8.33 and FDA expectations. Part II clauses 10.1-10.2 (closure integrity of fusion-sealed and other containers) were not found in the extracted text.

clause: Part VIII (oral solid dosage forms), 3.3-3.8 (compression in-process controls)
url: https://egazette.gov.in (G.S.R. 922(E)); text checked in user-supplied copy, lines 5532-5539, 5584-5592
requirement: Calibrated weighing equipment must be at hand for in-process tablet weight checks, with procedures able to catch out-of-limit tablets. At the start of each compression run, and for multi-station or multi-point machines at fixed intervals, enough individual tablets must be examined so that each station/point is checked for pharmacopoeial parameters (appearance, weight variation, disintegration, hardness, friability, thickness), with results recorded in the batch documentation. During compression, samples must be taken at intervals of no more than thirty minutes against the in-process specification, with periodic checks of the same parameters plus contamination by lubricating oil. Tablets must be de-dusted (preferably automatically) and checked for foreign matter and defects, collected in clean labelled containers, and rejected or discarded tablets must be kept in identified containers with their quantity recorded in the BMR.
system_implications: Compression step template with: start-of-run per-station/per-punch checks; an IPC timer that forces a sample entry at most every 30 minutes (configurable downward, never upward for India-market products); parameter set configurable per pharmacopoeia (IP/BP/USP limits for weight variation, DT, friability, hardness and thickness as in-house limits); balance calibration status check; reject/discard tablet quantities recorded and included in yield reconciliation; lubricant-oil contamination check field.
verification_test: Run compression for 45 minutes without an IPC entry and confirm the system raises a missed-IPC alarm/deviation at 30 minutes; for a 16-station press confirm the start-of-run check cannot be signed until each station has a result; confirm rejected tablet quantity feeds the yield calculation.
note: confirmed in official text. The fixed maximum 30-minute IPC interval and the named parameter list are Indian specifics; FDA 211.110 and EU Chapter 5 leave frequency to the firm.

clause: Part VIII, 2.1-2.5 (sifting, mixing, granulation) and 1.3-1.4
url: https://egazette.gov.in (G.S.R. 922(E)); text checked in user-supplied copy, lines 5566-5577, 5692-5698
requirement: Critical operating parameters such as time and temperature for every mixing, blending and drying step must be defined in the master formula, watched while the step runs and written into the batch record. Unless closed, mixing, sifting and blending equipment needs dust extraction or a dedicated area. Sieve residues must be examined periodically for foreign material. Fluid-bed drier filter bags must be washed between products, and product-dedicated for certain highly potent or sensitising products; inlet air must be filtered. Granulation and coating solutions must be made, stored and used so as to limit contamination and microbial growth. All dry ingredients are sifted before use (normally in dedicated areas) unless input quality is assured. A metal detector is recommended, wooden equipment is to be avoided, and screens, sieves, punches and dies must be checked for wear or breakage before and after each use.
system_implications: MBR step types for sifting, dry mixing, granulation, drying (FBD/tray), blending and lubrication with typed CPP fields (time, temperature, impeller/chopper speed, inlet/outlet air temperature, LOD) and limits; FBD filter-bag ID and product-dedication check; sieve integrity check before and after use with sieve ID and mesh; punch and die inspection record before and after each use; metal-detector challenge records; solution preparation time and hold-time limits.
verification_test: Enter a drying outlet temperature outside the MBR range and confirm a deviation prompt; try to use an FBD bag registered to another product and confirm it is blocked unless a washing record exists (or blocked outright for a dedicated-bag product); confirm the sieve integrity check is required both before and after sifting.
note: confirmed in official text. Before-and-after-use checks of sieves, punches and dies and the explicit FBD-bag rule are more prescriptive than FDA or EU texts.

clause: Part VIII, 4 (coating), 5 (capsule filling), 6 (printing of tablets and capsules)
url: https://egazette.gov.in (G.S.R. 922(E)); text checked in user-supplied copy, lines 5540-5551, 5739-5742
requirement: Air supplied to coating pans for drying must be filtered and of suitable quality, with exhaust and temperature/humidity control in the area. Coating solutions and suspensions are made fresh and used so as to minimise microbial growth, and their preparation and use are documented. Empty capsule shells count as a drug component and must be stored away from excess heat and moisture. Printing on tablets or capsules needs special care against mix-ups, with segregation if different products or batches are printed at the same time, edible-grade colours and suitable inks; printed tablets or capsules must be approved by QC before release for packaging or sale.
system_implications: Coating step template recording solution preparation time, use-by time, spray rate, inlet/exhaust temperatures and room temperature/RH; capsule shells handled as a component lot with storage-condition checks; a QC approval gate between tablet/capsule printing and packaging.
verification_test: Try to use coating suspension past its configured use-by time and confirm it is blocked; confirm a packaging order for a printed tablet cannot start until a QC approval of the printed bulk is recorded.
note: confirmed in official text. The QC approval gate after printing is an explicit Indian requirement not found in FDA/EU text.

clause: Part VIII, 7.1-7.4 (strip and blister packaging)
url: https://egazette.gov.in (G.S.R. 922(E)); text checked in user-supplied copy, lines 5743-5753
requirement: Automatic counting, strip and blister machines must be cleared of every 'rogue' tablet, capsule or foil before a new packaging operation, and an independent, recorded check of the equipment is required before a new batch is handled. Uncoated tablets are packed on equipment designed to limit cross-contamination, in an isolated area for potent or beta-lactam tablets. Strips leaving the machine are inspected for misprints, cut foil, missing tablets and poor sealing. Strip and blister pocket integrity must be checked periodically by a vacuum (leak) test, with records.
system_implications: Line-clearance for blister/strip lines needs a second, independent verifier signature (different user from the performer); packaging IPC template with defect categories (misprint, foil cut, empty pocket, seal) and a periodic leak-test step with frequency, sample size and pass/fail; product attributes 'uncoated', 'potent', 'beta-lactam' drive line/area eligibility.
verification_test: Attempt to sign both 'performed' and 'verified' for blister line clearance with the same user and confirm refusal; skip the scheduled leak test and confirm the packaging record flags a missed IPC; try to schedule a beta-lactam product on a non-isolated line and confirm it is blocked.
note: confirmed in official text. The independent recorded equipment check and periodic vacuum leak testing of blisters are explicit Indian rules; FDA/EU cover them only generally.

clause: Part VIII, 1.5, 1.14, 1.17, 1.25, 1.27-1.28 (pressure cascades, temperature and humidity)
url: https://egazette.gov.in (G.S.R. 922(E)); text checked in user-supplied copy, lines 5699-5702, 5728-5733, 5795-5798, 5810-5829
requirement: Where rooms are designed with pressure differentials, these must be monitored regularly and any deviation reported at once to Production and QA. Pressure-differential limits of adjacent rooms must not overlap. Pressure control and monitoring devices must be calibrated and qualified, compliance verified regularly and recorded, and alarms set from risk analysis. Room pressure indicators must show normal range and alert/action limits at the point of reading. Where relevant, temperature and relative humidity must be controlled, monitored and recorded, with alert and action limits.
system_implications: Tablets eBMR steps carry room ID and capture differential pressure, temperature and RH at start (and during long steps), manually or from the BMS/EMS, compared with room-specific alert/action limits; excursions notify Production and QA and link to the batch as a deviation; product-specific humidity limits for moisture-sensitive products.
verification_test: Enter a differential pressure below the action limit at a compression start and confirm the step is blocked or a deviation is opened and QA/Production are notified; confirm RH captured during granulation is printed in the batch record.
note: confirmed in official text (drawn from WHO HVAC guidance for non-sterile products); FDA/EU expect similar control but without this detail.

text: QR/barcode rules for finished formulations (Drugs Rules, Rule 96 and Schedule H2): G.S.R. 823(E) of 17 Nov 2022 required the 300 brands listed in Schedule H2 to carry a barcode or QR code on the primary pack label (secondary if space is short) from 1 Aug 2023, encoding: unique product identification code, proper and generic name, brand name, manufacturer name and address, batch number, manufacturing date, expiry date and manufacturing licence number. G.S.R. 506(E) of 22 Jun 2026 (Drugs (Seventh Amendment) Rules 2026, after a draft of 16 Oct 2025) extends Schedule H2 to whole categories: all vaccines, NDPS narcotic and psychotropic drugs and anticancer drugs from 1 Jul 2027, and all antimicrobials from 1 Jul 2028; reports say the code must also carry excipient details where applicable.
url: https://www.business-standard.com/industry/news/govt-mandates-qr-codes-for-vaccines-antimicrobials-and-cancer-drugs-126062500620_1.html
note: 2022 rule confirmed by several sources (IDMA FAQ, CliniExperts, TheHealthMaster); 2026 amendment consistent across Business Standard, Medical Dialogues, RAPS and others. Official gazette text not read (egazette blocked); the exact excipient data element wording needs confirmation.

text: API QR code: G.S.R. 20(E) of 18 Jan 2022 requires every API made in or imported into India to carry a QR code at each packaging level from 1 Jan 2023, holding unique product identification code, API name, brand name if any, manufacturer name and address, batch number, batch size, manufacturing date, expiry or retest date, serial shipping container code, manufacturing or import licence number and special storage conditions.
url: https://thehealthmaster.com/2022/01/21/govt-mandates-qr-code-on-labels-of-all-apis-manufactured-and-imported/

text: DGFT export track-and-trace (barcoding of tertiary, secondary and primary packs for exported formulations, data upload to the iVEDA portal) was withdrawn by DGFT Public Notice 44/2024-25 of 31 Jan 2025, which removed para 2.76 of the Handbook of Procedures 2023. Tertiary (2011) and secondary (2013) barcoding had been in force; primary-level barcoding and parent-child uploads had been deferred repeatedly (last to 1 Feb 2025). Authentication of exported formulations is left to MoHFW under the Drugs Rules; no replacement export-specific Indian rule was found as of Sep 2026. Exporters must instead meet destination-country serialisation (US DSCSA, EU FMD).

why: For domestic packs of a Schedule H2 brand, and from 1 Jul 2027/2028 for all vaccines, NDPS drugs, anticancer drugs and antimicrobials, the packaging record must show that the correct code was printed on the primary (or secondary) label and verified. The eBPR should generate the payload from batch master data and record reader verification results.
