clause: Part I, 17.3.10.5, 17.3.10.16-17.3.10.17 (equipment SOPs and logs) and 18.4.3, 18.4.9 (equipment failure, calibration)
url: https://egazette.gov.in (G.S.R. 922(E)); text checked in user-supplied copy, lines 1430-1434, 1463-1467, 1507-1508, 1646-1650, 1867-1869
requirement: Each instrument and piece of equipment needs SOPs (use, calibration, cleaning, maintenance) kept close to it. Records must be kept for major and critical equipment of validations, calibrations, maintenance, cleaning and repairs with dates and who did them, and use of major/critical equipment and of processing areas must be logged in chronological order. There must be a means of signalling equipment or utility failures; defective equipment is withdrawn until fixed; equipment is cleaned promptly after use and stored clean and dry. Measuring, weighing, recording and control instruments are serviced and calibrated at set intervals with records, checked daily or before use for analytical tests, and labelled with the calibration date and next due date.
system_implications: Electronic equipment and room logbooks populated automatically from batch execution (who, what product/batch, start/end, cleaning, maintenance), chronological and non-editable except via audited corrections; equipment status (qualified, calibrated, cleaned, out of service) checked before any step can use it; daily balance verification records; calibration due-date blocking.
verification_test: Use a balance whose calibration is past due and confirm the weighing step is blocked; mark a blender 'out of service' and confirm no batch can select it; export the equipment log for a granulator and confirm entries are chronological and include batch numbers and users.
note: confirmed in official text (FDA 211.67/211.68/211.182 and EU 3.x/4.31-4.32 are equivalent).

clause: Part I, 18.4.4 (time limits after cleaning) and 18.4.5, 18.2.8
url: https://egazette.gov.in (G.S.R. 922(E)); text checked in user-supplied copy, lines 1438-1444, 1805-1807
requirement: Time limits for storing process materials and cleaned equipment before use must be stated and based on data. Containers for filling must be cleaned before filling, with attention to glass fragments and metal particles. In-process controls done in production areas must not harm the product or another product.
system_implications: Clean-hold-time (and dirty-hold-time where defined) per equipment class, validated and stored in master data; the system computes 'clean status valid until' and blocks use after expiry, forcing re-cleaning; process-material hold times as in SM-11/SM-13.
verification_test: Clean a tablet press, wait past its validated clean-hold time (simulated clock) and confirm the next batch cannot use it until it is re-cleaned.
note: confirmed in official text

clause: Part I, section 8 (change control), 8.1-8.7
url: https://egazette.gov.in (G.S.R. 922(E)); text checked in user-supplied copy, lines 79-83, 744, 788-789, 806-811, 828-829, 848-850, 904-905
requirement: A formal change-control system must assess all changes that could affect production and control. Written procedures must govern how changes are identified, documented, reviewed and approved, whether they concern materials and their specifications, test methods, buildings and utilities, equipment, process steps, labels and packs, or computer hardware and software. Proposals are drafted, reviewed and approved by the relevant units and by the quality units. Impact on product quality is evaluated, and changes may be classified (e.g., minor/major) to decide testing and validation. All affected documents must be revised when the change is implemented. The first batch made or tested after the change must be evaluated, and effects of critical changes on retest or expiry dates assessed (possibly with accelerated or ongoing stability).
system_implications: Every MBR/MPR version, equipment or software configuration change references an approved change record; the system flags the 'first batch after change' for mandatory post-change evaluation by QA and can route it to stability; eBMR software and configuration changes themselves follow change control (see SM-10).
verification_test: Approve an MBR revision under change record CC-1 and confirm the first batch executed on it is flagged 'post-change evaluation required' and cannot be released until that evaluation is signed.
note: confirmed in official text. The explicit first-batch evaluation (from ICH Q7) is not written into 21 CFR 211 or EU Chapter 1 for finished products, though EU 1.4(xii)/ICH Q10 expect post-implementation evaluation.

clause: Part I, section 10 (self-inspection, quality audits, suppliers), 10.1-10.8
url: https://egazette.gov.in (G.S.R. 922(E)); text checked in user-supplied copy, lines 302-343, 530-534, 567-572, 585-593
requirement: Self-inspections must be routine and at least once a year (frequency stated in the procedure), done by an objective team of GMP-knowledgeable staff (internal or external), and may also be triggered by recalls, repeated rejections or announced inspections. A report must cover results, evaluation and conclusions and recommended corrective actions, with management follow-up; the self-inspection checklist covers documentation, production and IPCs, QC, sanitation, validation, complaints, recalls, labels control and results of previous self-inspections. Suppliers are approved by QC together with other departments after evaluation, audited where needed, and listed as approved.
system_implications: The eBMR should provide an audit mode for self-inspection (read-only access to records, sampling of batches, export of deviations/CAPA status) and link CAPA from self-inspection findings; approved-supplier list is master data used by dispensing (SM-20).
verification_test: Create a self-inspection finding referencing three batch records and confirm the linked CAPA and batch references are traceable both ways; confirm an auditor role can view but not modify batch records.
note: confirmed in official text. A fixed minimum of one self-inspection per year is stricter than 21 CFR 211 (no self-inspection clause) and EU Chapter 9 (no fixed frequency).

clause: Part I, sections 6 (complaints and adverse reactions) and 7 (product recalls)
requirement: Complaints about possible defects are recorded in full, investigated (normally with the QC head), and all decisions and measures recorded and cross-referenced to the batch records; other batches, including any containing reprocessed material from the defective batch, must be considered; complaint records are reviewed for trends; the licensing authority is told when action is contemplated for serious quality problems. A pharmacovigilance system must collect and forward ADR reports to the licensing authorities. Recalls: written SOP able to reach every distribution level down to retail quickly (print and electronic media may be used); the authorised person runs recalls; distribution records with wholesaler and direct-customer details must be readily available; recalled stock is segregated securely; the licensing authority is informed of any intended recall; progress is recorded and a final report reconciles delivered and recovered quantities; recall arrangements are tested periodically.
system_implications: Batch genealogy must answer 'which batches share this material lot or contain reprocessed/recovered material from batch X' in seconds; complaint and recall records link to batch IDs; distribution data (customer, quantity, date) per batch available for recall reconciliation.
verification_test: Given a defective API lot, list all finished batches using it, including batches containing recovered material from affected batches; generate a recall reconciliation for one batch showing distributed vs returned quantities.
note: confirmed in official text

clause: Part I, 11.2, 11.4 (training), 11.5 (personal hygiene)
url: https://egazette.gov.in (G.S.R. 922(E)); text checked in user-supplied copy, lines 105-138, 165-168, 179-240, 418-434
requirement: Staff must be qualified and trained, with written job descriptions, an organisation chart, no gaps or unexplained overlaps in GMP responsibilities, and deputies only if suitably qualified. Training follows a written programme for everyone entering production or QC areas, including maintenance and cleaning staff; there is job-specific training for new recruits, continuing training with periodic assessment of effectiveness, specific training for clean areas and hazardous materials, and training records (including evidence of qualification for consultants and contract staff). Health checks are required before and during employment, with periodic eye checks for visual inspectors; sick staff with lesions are excluded from handling products; untrained visitors are kept out or supervised.
system_implications: User qualification matrix: each MBR step type requires a training record (and, for inspectors, a current eye test); the system refuses sign-on or step execution by untrained users and records training status at the time of signature; visitor/contractor accounts are read-only or supervised.
verification_test: Assign a compression step to a user without the compression training record and confirm it is refused; let an operator's training expire mid-campaign and confirm new steps are blocked while earlier signatures remain valid.
note: confirmed in official text

clause: Part I, section 9 (production under loan licence or contract, contract analysis), 9.1-9.5
requirement: Production under a loan licence or contract must follow the product licence and a written contract that sets each party's responsibilities (including release, sampling and testing) and states how the authorised person releases each batch. Only a holder of a valid manufacturing licence may manufacture under contract; subcontracting needs the contract giver's prior approval. The loan licensee or contract giver must review records and results, confirm GMP and licence compliance and release by the authorised person, and must hold or have access to manufacturing, analytical and distribution records and reference samples, including any needed for complaints or suspected fraud.
system_implications: Multi-party batch model: a batch can belong to a loan licensee (the brand owner's licence) while made on the facility's premises; batch records must carry both parties' licence numbers and allow controlled, read-only sharing with the loan licensee/contract giver; release workflow configurable to show which party's authorised person releases.
verification_test: Create a loan-licence batch and confirm the record shows the loan licence number and the host manufacturing licence number, and that a contract-giver reviewer can view but not edit the completed record.
note: confirmed in official text. 'Loan licence' is an Indian legal construct (Drugs Rules Forms 25A/28A) without an exact FDA/EU equivalent; EU Chapter 7 covers outsourced activities.

clause: Part I, section 5 (qualification and validation), 5.1-5.12; Appendix I (site master file) item on computerised-system validation
url: https://egazette.gov.in (G.S.R. 922(E)); text checked in user-supplied copy, lines 574-577, 602-605, 612, 653-699, 724-725, 858-860, 938-940, 2376-2377
requirement: Each company must identify the qualification and validation needed to show critical aspects are controlled, in a validation master plan covering DQ, IQ, OQ, PQ and process validation, per approved protocols, with written reports; any change that may affect quality must be qualified or validated; validation is ongoing with periodic review, and processes are set on validation results. Particular attention goes to analytical methods, automated systems and cleaning procedures. The site master file must describe qualification and calibration, including recording systems and arrangements for computerised-system validation.
system_implications: The eBMR (an automated system) must be included in the customer's VMP; vendor should supply validation deliverables and support periodic review; the site master file section on computerised systems will describe the eBMR, so the vendor should provide a short, accurate system description.
verification_test: Check the validation package contains URS, risk assessment, IQ/OQ scripts, traceability matrix and a periodic-review template; check a site-master-file text snippet describing the eBMR is available.
note: confirmed in official text

clause: Part I, 19.1-19.7 (quality control: independence, basic requirements, sampling, OOS, material release)
url: https://egazette.gov.in (G.S.R. 922(E)); text checked in user-supplied copy, lines 1673-1735, 1745-1751, 2310-2328
requirement: QC must be independent of production and other departments and headed by a suitably qualified person. Samples are taken by QC-approved methods and people; records (manual or instrument) must show all sampling and testing was done and deviations investigated; product assessment must include review of production documentation and deviations; finished products must match the licensed composition. Tests follow written procedures and results are checked by a supervisor before release or rejection. Sample containers are labelled with material name, batch, container number, sample number, sampler's signature and date. Out-of-specification results must be investigated under an approved procedure and recorded. Before releasing starting or packaging materials the QC in-charge must ensure testing for identity, strength, purity and other quality parameters.
system_implications: IPC results captured in the eBMR that are specification tests must follow the same OOS workflow as QC results (no silent retest); sampling steps in the eBMR generate labelled samples with sampler identity; batch release requires QC result approval by a checker different from the analyst.
verification_test: Enter an IPC assay result outside specification and confirm the system opens an OOS investigation and blocks further dependent steps; try to replace the result by re-entering a passing value and confirm the original remains in the record and the OOS stays open.
note: confirmed in official text up to 19.7.1; the text after '19.7.2 An identity test shall be...' is cut off in the extracted copy, so later QC clauses (possibly retained samples, stability, finished-product release details) were not checked.

source: Revised Schedule M (G.S.R. 922(E), 2023) and Drugs Rules 1945, Rules 74 and 78 (conditions of licence)
clause: Part I, 19.3(g) (retained samples); Drugs Rules Rule 74 (Form 25 licences) and Rule 78 (Form 28 licences) reference-sample conditions
url: https://indiankanoon.org/doc/130533556/ (Rule 74; blocked, read via search summaries); Schedule M text checked in user-supplied copy, lines 1693-1696
requirement: Schedule M requires enough samples of starting materials and products to be retained for future examination, kept for an appropriate time in the final pack (or an equivalent pack if the marketed one is very large). The conditions of licence in the Drugs Rules set the amount and period: at least twice the quantity needed for all tests on the batch, kept for three months beyond the expiry date, or three years from manufacture where no expiry is labelled.
system_implications: The packaging record should create the reference/retention sample pull with a quantity computed from the test plan (at least 2x full testing), and the sample-retention date must be the maximum across target markets: India expiry + 3 months, FDA 211.170 expiry + 1 year, EU Annex 19 expiry + 1 year (and for EU at least 2 years after release for some starting materials).
verification_test: For a batch sold in India and the US, confirm the sample retention date is expiry + 1 year; for an India-only batch confirm expiry + 3 months (unless company policy is stricter); confirm pull quantity is at least twice the full test quantity.
note: Schedule M part confirmed in official text; the Rule 74/78 quantity and 3-month period come from search summaries of Rule 74 (primary sites blocked). India is LESS strict than FDA/EU on retention period, so the foreign rule governs exported batches.

source: Drugs Rules 1945, Rule 74 and Rule 78 (conditions of licence) with Schedule U
clause: Rule 74 (records of manufacture per Schedule U; records of tests) and Rule 78 equivalents
url: https://indiankanoon.org/doc/130533556/ (blocked; via search summaries)
requirement: Separately from Schedule M, the conditions of a manufacturing licence require batch-wise manufacturing records with the particulars listed in Schedule U (e.g., product name, batch size and number, dates of start and completion of manufacture, ingredients and quantities, raw-material control numbers, analytical report references, actual production and packing details, date of release for sale) and records of tests, kept for five years (reported as from the date of manufacture). Summaries of Rule 78 (Schedule C/C(1) products on Form 28) describe test records kept for two years after expiry for products with an expiry date and five years from manufacture for others.
system_implications: India retention rule for batch records should be computed as the longest of: Schedule M (expiry + 1 year), Rule 74/78 (5 years from manufacture, or expiry + 2 years where Rule 78 applies), plus EU (5 years after certification) and FDA (expiry + 1 year) for exported batches. The Schedule U particulars (including 'date of release for distribution or sale') must appear in the eBMR.
verification_test: For a 24-month shelf-life tablet made in 2026, confirm the retention date is at least 2031 (manufacture + 5 years) rather than 2029 (expiry + 1 year); for a Form 28 injectable with 36-month shelf life confirm at least expiry + 2 years.
note: Not in Schedule M; based on consistent search summaries of Rules 74 and 78 (indiankanoon, cdsco.gov.in blocked). Verify exact clause letters and the Rule 78 periods against the current Drugs Rules compilation before use.

source: Drugs Rules 1945, Rule 71 and Rule 76 (conditions for grant of licence) with Schedule M 11.3.2
clause: Rule 71(1)/Rule 76 (competent technical staff; testing staff); Schedule M Part I 11.3.2
url: https://indiankanoon.org/doc/153309436/ (blocked; via search summaries); Schedule M text checked in user-supplied copy, lines 385-402
requirement: Manufacture must be carried out under the active direction and personal supervision of competent technical staff (at least one whole-time person with prescribed pharmacy, science, chemical engineering or medical qualifications and experience), and testing under qualified staff approved by the licensing authority. Schedule M says key personnel must hold the qualifications and experience specified under the rules.
system_implications: Maintain a register of 'approved technical staff' (production and testing) with the licensing-authority approval reference and date; restrict production-supervisor and QC approval signatures in the eBMR to approved persons for Indian licences; changes in approved staff must be reportable.
verification_test: Remove a user from the approved-technical-staff register and confirm they can no longer sign as production supervisor or QC approver on India-licensed batches, while operator-level signatures remain possible.
note: Rule 71 content from search summaries (primary blocked); Schedule M 11.3.2 cross-reference confirmed in official text. EU has the QP, FDA has no named-person approval; Indian 'approved staff' are named on or approved against the licence.

clause: Part XII (APIs, ICH Q7-based), 6.1 documentation clauses (e-signature sentence, probably 6.1.9), 6.1.5-6.1.7
url: https://egazette.gov.in (G.S.R. 922(E)); text checked in user-supplied copy, lines 6811, 6851-6853, 6942-6957
requirement: The only explicit electronic-signature rule in Schedule M sits in the API Part: where electronic signatures are used on documents they must be authenticated and secure. The same Part requires entries made indelibly right after the activity, identifying the person, with corrections dated and signed leaving the original readable; records may be kept as originals or accurate copies, and where electronic records are used there must be retrieval equipment and a way to produce a hard copy; records must be readily available at the site during retention, or promptly retrievable electronically.
system_implications: Although Part XII legally governs API manufacture, it is the clearest Indian statement of e-signature expectations and should be applied in both editions: unique credentials, re-authentication at signing, signature bound to the record, tamper-evidence, and on-demand human-readable hard copy/PDF of any record with signatures and audit trail.
verification_test: Sign a step, then alter the underlying value via direct database access in a test environment and confirm the signature verification reports the record as altered; print a completed batch record and confirm signatures show name, date/time and meaning.
note: confirmed in official text; clause number 6.1.9 inferred from ICH Q7 ordering. For dosage forms, Part I relies on 'signature or electronic password' (SM-14) and the data-processing clause (SM-09).

clause: Part XIII, item 11 (parenteral preparations: areas, equipment, minimum areas) and FFS/BFS subsection
url: https://egazette.gov.in (G.S.R. 922(E)); text checked in user-supplied copy, lines 8546-8760, 8801-8854
requirement: For parenterals, Part XIII divides operations into separate areas (water management, container and closure preparation, solution preparation, filling/capping/sealing, sterilisation, quarantine, visual inspection, packaging; FFS/BFS lines have their own list) and recommends equipment for each, e.g., RO or EDI plus multi-column distillation, SS 316L storage tank and continuously circulating loop, automatic washers, double-ended dryer/steriliser, cartridge/membrane filtration, filling under laminar air flow, steam steriliser preferably with computer-controlled cycles, hot-air steriliser, pressure leak tester, visual inspection units with white and black backgrounds and lighting, batch coding machine and labelling unit. Recommended minimum areas are about 150 m2 basic plus 100 m2 ancillary for SVI, 150 m2 each for LVP, 100 m2 for LVP packaging materials, and 250 m2 plus 150 m2 for FFS LVP lines, partitioned with airlocks.
system_implications: Injectables edition master data should offer these area types and equipment classes out of the box (so MBR steps can reference them), including leak-test and visual-inspection equipment classes, and record the WFI loop/point-of-use for each water draw.
verification_test: Build an SVI MBR using only standard area/equipment classes and confirm every Part XIII area type needed is available; confirm a leak-test step can only reference equipment of the 'pressure leak tester' class.
note: confirmed in official text (list is fragmentary after extraction). Prescriptive minimum areas and equipment lists have no FDA/EU counterpart. The Part XIII tablet section (referred to as 'item 3 of Tablet') did not survive extraction.

clause: Part I (PQS resources list; 15.2 reference standards; 17.3.2 specifications; packaging-material clause) - Indian Pharmacopoeia references
url: https://egazette.gov.in (G.S.R. 922(E)); text checked in user-supplied copy, lines 661-666, 1916-1917, 2180-2183, 2285-2295
requirement: The PQS must make the key reference texts available, expressly the 1940 Act and 1945 Rules, the latest IP edition and official MoHFW guidance documents. Specifications may need periodic revision to follow new editions of the IP or other official pharmacopoeias. IP reference standards must be obtained from the Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission. Packaging materials must meet IP requirements, and purified water must meet pharmacopoeial specifications (potable water per BIS or municipal standards as feed).
system_implications: Specifications and IPC limits in the MBR must reference a pharmacopoeia and edition (IP 2022, IP 2026, USP, Ph. Eur., BP) as data; an edition change (e.g., IP 2026 effective 1 Jul 2026) must trigger change control of affected MBR limits; the product's target markets decide which pharmacopoeia governs each test, with the stricter limit applied where a batch serves several markets.
verification_test: Mark IP 2026 as effective on 1 Jul 2026 and confirm the system lists all MBRs whose IPC limits cite IP 2022 for review; for a product sold in India and the US, confirm each IPC limit shows its source pharmacopoeia and that the narrower range is enforced.
note: confirmed in official text. IP 2026 (10th edition) release on 2 Jan 2026 and effect from 1 Jul 2026 come from IPC/news searches, not the Schedule M text.

clause: Part III (hazardous substances: sex hormones, steroids, cytotoxics) general, 2 (risk assessment), 4 (PPE and breathing air)
url: https://egazette.gov.in (G.S.R. 922(E)); text checked in user-supplied copy, lines 3446-3468, 4132-4134, 4163-4205
requirement: Where a tablet or injectable contains sex hormones, steroids or cytotoxics, Part III applies in addition to Part I: a risk assessment must decide the hazard to operators, public and environment and which stages fall under Part III; facility and equipment should give containment, otherwise operator protection (suits, double gloves where contact is unavoidable, respirators with breathing air) is required; central breathing-air systems need a 100% back-up with automatic changeover; de-gowning and decontamination procedures apply.
system_implications: Product master data carries a hazard class that restricts which rooms, lines and equipment can be used and inserts PPE, containment-check and decontamination steps into the MBR automatically; the batch record should capture those checks.
verification_test: Classify a product as cytotoxic and confirm the MBR designer adds mandatory PPE and decontamination steps and only offers contained areas; try scheduling it on a general OSD line and confirm it is blocked.
note: confirmed in official text, but Part III text is heavily interleaved with biological-product text in the extracted copy, so detail should be rechecked against a clean copy.

source: Information Technology Act 2000 (as amended 2008), sections 3A, 4, 5, 7 and Second Schedule
clause: s.4 legal recognition of electronic records; s.5 legal recognition of electronic signatures; s.3A reliability criteria; s.7 retention of electronic records
url: https://www.indiacode.nic.in/bitstream/123456789/1999/1/A2000-21%20(1).pdf
requirement: Where a law requires information in writing, an electronic record satisfies it if it stays accessible for later reference (s.4). Where a law requires a signature, the requirement is met by an electronic signature affixed in the manner prescribed by the Central Government (s.5). An electronic signature technique is treated as reliable if the signing data is linked to and controlled by the signer alone and any later change to the signature or to the signed information is detectable (s.3A(2)); recognised techniques are listed in the Second Schedule (digital signatures under licensed certifying authorities, and Aadhaar/e-KYC based eSign). Where a law requires records to be retained, electronic retention qualifies if the information stays accessible, is kept in its original format or one shown to represent it accurately, and origin, destination and date/time details are kept (s.7).
system_implications: eBMR records satisfy s.4 and s.7 if kept readable in original or demonstrably faithful format with metadata (creator, time, source system). For signatures, design to the s.3A(2) reliability tests (unique credentials, sole control, tamper evidence via hashing/signing of record content). For the highest-stakes approvals (MBR approval, batch release by the authorised person) offer optional PKI digital signatures (Class 3 DSC from a licensed CA) or eSign to fall squarely within s.5; username/password signatures rely on Schedule M's own acceptance of 'signature or electronic password'.
verification_test: Verify an exported, signed batch record PDF: signature validation must detect any change to the document; confirm a DSC-signed release signature validates against the CCA root chain; confirm record metadata (origin system, timestamps) survives archive and restore.
note: Section content confirmed through several legal summaries and the India Code listing (primary PDF not fetched). Whether a password-based GMP e-signature is an 'electronic signature' under s.5 is an open legal point (see open questions).

source: Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023, section 63 (in force 1 Jul 2024; replaces Indian Evidence Act s.65B)
clause: s.63 admissibility of electronic records; certificate in the prescribed Schedule form
url: https://www.rkdewan.com/articles/electronic-records-now-governed-by-section-63-of-the-bhartiya-sakshya-adhiniyam-2023/
requirement: Computer output (printouts, copies on media) of an electronic record is treated as a document and admissible without the original if section 63 conditions are met; for such secondary electronic evidence a certificate in the prescribed form is needed, reportedly signed by the person in charge of the device and an expert and including a hash value of the record.
system_implications: To support prosecutions or defence under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act (e.g., NSQ or spurious drug cases), the eBMR should be able to produce a certified export of any batch record: rendered copy plus machine-readable data, a cryptographic hash (e.g., SHA-256) of each exported file, and system/operation details needed for the s.63 certificate.
verification_test: Export a batch record with its audit trail and confirm the export manifest lists SHA-256 hashes that re-verify, plus system name, version, time source and operator details needed to fill the certificate.
note: BSA s.63 facts from multiple legal summaries; exact certificate format not reviewed (open question).

source: Indian Pharmacopoeia (uniformity of weight) vs USP, applied through Revised Schedule M Part VIII 3.4 ('pharmacopoeial parameters')
clause: Part VIII 3.4 and 3.8 (weight variation checks against pharmacopoeial parameters); IP general test for uniformity of weight
url: https://pharmatreasures.blogspot.com/2012/05/tablet-weight-variation-and-uniformity.html
requirement: Part VIII requires in-process checks of weight variation and other pharmacopoeial parameters, which for Indian products means IP limits. IP (like BP/Ph. Eur.) sets average-weight bands of 80 mg or less (10% deviation), above 80 mg and under 250 mg (7.5%) and 250 mg or more (5%), whereas the older USP weight-variation bands commonly used as in-process limits are 130 mg or less (10%), 130-324 mg (7.5%) and above 324 mg (5%); current USP <905> instead judges uniformity of dosage units by an acceptance value. The same tablet can therefore fall in different bands (e.g., a 200 mg tablet: 7.5% under both; a 300 mg tablet: 5% under IP but 7.5% under old-USP bands).
system_implications: Weight-variation limits must be computed from the tablet's target weight using a pharmacopoeia-specific band table (IP/BP/Ph. Eur. vs USP), stored as versioned reference data, and the MBR must show which table applies; for multi-market products apply the tighter band. Also allow a separate harmonised UDU (acceptance value) calculation for release testing.
verification_test: For a 300 mg tablet, confirm the India (IP) configuration gives +/-5% individual limits while a USP-only configuration using the legacy bands gives +/-7.5%, and a product sold in both uses +/-5%; for 100 mg confirm IP 7.5% vs USP legacy 10%.
note: Band values from several secondary sources (not the IP text itself). IPC published a draft harmonised 'Uniformity of Dosage Units' chapter (Oct 2024) and IP 2026 took effect 1 Jul 2026, so confirm the current IP 2026 wording before hard-coding.

clause: Part II, 3.1-3.4 (sanitation of clean areas, disinfectants) and 5.9 (water monitoring)
url: https://egazette.gov.in (G.S.R. 922(E)); text checked in user-supplied copy, lines 3079-3080, 3095-3097, 3197, 3227-3232, 2863-2866
requirement: Clean areas must be cleaned often and thoroughly under an approved programme; disinfectants, where used, must be of at least two kinds, and the programme must include a sporicidal agent; effectiveness must be demonstrated, interactions between cleaning agents validated and disinfectant residues shown to be removed. Disinfectants and detergents are monitored for microbial contamination, dilutions kept in cleaned containers and stored only for defined periods unless sterilised, and those for Grade A/B areas must be sterile before use. Fumigation may help for inaccessible places. Water sources, treatment equipment and treated water are monitored regularly for chemical, microbial and endotoxin contamination, with records of results and actions.
system_implications: Cleaning/sanitisation records for Grade A-D rooms and equipment should record agent, lot, dilution preparation time and expiry, sterility status for A/B use, and rotation; the batch record should link to the cleaning events covering the batch window; water test results (WFI endotoxin, TOC, conductivity, microbial) for points used by the batch should be viewable at release.
verification_test: Record use of a disinfectant dilution beyond its defined storage period and confirm it is rejected; confirm the batch review screen lists the WFI points used and their latest results relative to the batch dates.
note: confirmed in official text

clause: Part II, 4.5 (HEPA filter leak testing), 4.6 (classification sampling)
url: https://egazette.gov.in (G.S.R. 922(E)); text checked in user-supplied copy, lines 2950-2966, 2980-2983, 3192-3195
requirement: Installed HEPA filters must be leak-tested to ISO standards, recommended every six months and never more than twelve months apart, using an aerosol that does not support microbial growth; patching is allowed within ISO limits. For classification, Grade A needs at least 1 m3 per location; lower grades at least 2 litres and one minute per location; portable counters with short tubing and isokinetic heads in unidirectional flow.
system_implications: Room/HEPA master data holds last and next leak-test dates; the injectables eBMR should warn or block use of a Grade A/B room whose HEPA test is overdue (more than 12 months, or more than 6 months if the site adopts the recommendation).
verification_test: Set a filling room's HEPA test date to 13 months ago and confirm batches cannot start in that room; at 7 months confirm a warning if the site profile follows the 6-month recommendation.
note: confirmed in official text. The explicit 6-12 month interval is more prescriptive than EU Annex 1 (2022), which leaves frequency to the contamination control strategy; FDA's aseptic guidance suggests twice-yearly testing.

clause: Part I, 18.3.1-18.3.5 (prevention of cross-contamination) and 18.2.4, 18.2.7, 18.5.1
requirement: Cross-contamination must be prevented by technical or organisational measures: dedicated self-contained areas (which may be needed for penicillins, cytotoxics, sex hormones, spore-formers, live vaccines and some biologicals), or campaign production followed by validated cleaning, airlocks and pressure differentials, limiting recirculation of untreated air, protective clothing, cleaning of known effectiveness, closed systems, residue testing and cleanliness status labels on equipment; effectiveness is checked periodically. Two products may share a room at the same time or back-to-back only when mix-up and cross-contamination risks are excluded; non-medicinal products may not be made in drug areas or equipment; different products are not packed in close proximity without physical segregation. Dust generation from dry materials must be controlled.
system_implications: Scheduling/eligibility rules: product-to-room and product-to-equipment restrictions (dedicated, campaign-only), campaign length and end-of-campaign cleaning validation references; prevent two open batches of different products in the same room unless the room is configured as segregated; residue test results (swab/rinse) as a gate before changeover.
verification_test: Try to start a second product in a room that already has an open step for another product and confirm refusal; end a campaign and confirm the next product cannot start until the validated changeover cleaning and residue results are recorded.
note: confirmed in official text

clause: Part I, 14.21-14.25 (packaging materials) and 14.36 (returned goods)
url: https://egazette.gov.in (G.S.R. 922(E)); text checked in user-supplied copy, lines 1163-1167, 1200-1202, 2246-2247, 2258-2270, 2272-2273
requirement: Primary and printed packaging materials are bought, handled and controlled like starting materials. Printed materials are stored securely against unauthorised access, roll-feed labels preferred, cut labels and loose printed items kept and moved in separate closed containers, and issued only by designated staff under an approved, documented procedure. Every packaging lot or delivery is given a unique identifier; outdated or obsolete material is destroyed with a record. Returned products are destroyed unless their quality is certain, and are reissued, relabelled or otherwise dealt with only after a documented QC assessment considering product nature, storage needs, condition, history and time since issue.
system_implications: Printed packaging components are lot-controlled with artwork version; issue to a packaging order only by a designated role with scan confirmation against the MPR bill of materials and artwork version; obsolete artwork versions are blocked and destruction recorded; returned-goods disposition workflow with QC assessment before any reuse.
verification_test: Try to issue cartons printed with a superseded artwork version to a packaging order and confirm the scan is rejected; confirm returned stock cannot be moved to 'available' without a QC assessment record.
note: confirmed in official text

field: Manufacturing licence number and licence form (e.g., Form 25 for tablets and other non-Schedule C/C(1) drugs; Form 28, or 28-D for LVPs, sera and vaccines, for parenterals, which are Schedule C drugs; Form 25-F/28 variants for Schedule X), plus the loan licence number (Form 25-A/28-A) when made under a loan licence
why: Printed on every label as 'Mfg. Lic. No.' and held in the BMR/BPR header; it identifies the licensed premises and the legal regime (Rule 74 vs Rule 78 conditions, which differ on retention). Loan-licence batches must show both the loan licensee's licence and the host facility. It is also one of the Schedule H2 QR data elements.
legal_basis: Drugs Rules 1945 Rule 96 (labelling), Rules 69/70, 74/75 and 76/78 (licences and conditions), Schedule A forms; Revised Schedule M Part I section 9 (loan licence)

field: Date of manufacture (month and year) in uncoded form on labels and in the batch record, alongside expiry date preceded by 'Expiry date'/'Exp.'
why: Schedule M's minimum label content includes both expiry and manufacture date in plain form, and Rule 96 requires both; EU and US labels do not require a manufacturing date, so the eBPR coding check must verify it only for India-market packs.
legal_basis: Revised Schedule M Part I 17.3.1 (finished drug labels); Drugs Rules Rule 96

field: Batch number with a Rule 96 prefix ('Batch No.', 'B. No.', 'Batch', 'Lot No.' or 'Lot'), related bulk and packing batch numbers, and a batch-number allocation log entry
why: Label format is prescribed; Schedule M 17.3.10.8-11 requires a numbering SOP linking processing and packaging numbers, never reusing a number (including after reprocessing), and logging each allocation.
legal_basis: Drugs Rules Rule 96; Revised Schedule M Part I 17.3.10.8-17.3.10.11 and 14.32

field: Maximum Retail Price (M.R.P., inclusive of all taxes) overprint for domestic packs
why: Domestic packs must carry the MRP; it is batch- or period-variable data overprinted during packaging, so the eBPR must capture the MRP value used, verify the overprint and reconcile coded packs. Formulations under the Drugs (Prices Control) Order are exempt from the Legal Metrology packaged-commodity declarations but not from the MRP display duty.
legal_basis: Drugs (Prices Control) Order 2013 under the Essential Commodities Act 1955 (MRP display); Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules 2011 exemption for DPCO formulations

field: Proper (generic) name with pharmacopoeial suffix 'I.P.' where the drug is in the Indian Pharmacopoeia, printed at least two font sizes larger than the brand name (combinations of three or more actives exempt)
why: Artwork verification in the master packaging record must check generic-name prominence and IP designation for India packs; this conflicts with some export market conventions, so artwork templates are market-specific.
legal_basis: Drugs Rules Rule 96(1)(i) as amended by the Drugs and Cosmetics (First Amendment) Rules 2018 (mandatory from 1 Apr 2019)

field: Schedule H, H1 or X caution text in a red-bordered box and Rx/NRx/XRx symbol at top left, per the drug's schedule classification
why: The product master must carry the Indian schedule classification so that the packaging record checks the correct caution panel on labels and cartons; FDA/EU have different prescription-status markings.
legal_basis: Drugs Rules Rule 97 and Schedules H, H1, X

field: Export-only label particulars: 'For export only - Not for domestic consumption' (as reported for export-only stock), plus name of drug, manufacturer name and address (or a licensing-authority-approved code number when the foreign consignee asks), licence number, batch number and expiry
why: Export packs follow the importing country's label law, but Rule 94 keeps certain Indian particulars mandatory; the eBPR must switch artwork checks by destination and record the approved code number where used.
legal_basis: Drugs Rules Rule 94 (packing and labelling of drugs for export)

field: Hold time permitted for each intermediate and in-process material, and actual hold durations
why: Explicitly required in both the master formula and the batch processing record under revised Schedule M; FDA/EU do not list it as a batch record element.
legal_basis: Revised Schedule M Part I 17.3.6.2 and 17.3.8

field: Named person accountable for each production stage, plus the dated sign-off of the processing lead when the record is completed
why: Schedule M lists these as batch processing record elements; the eBMR must model a 'stage responsible person' separately from step performers and verifiers.
legal_basis: Revised Schedule M Part I 17.3.8 (batch processing records)

field: Approved technical staff identity (production and testing) with licensing-authority approval reference
why: Manufacture must be under the active direction and personal supervision of approved competent technical staff, and testing under approved analytical staff; supervisory and QC approval signatures on Indian-licensed batches should be limited to these persons.
legal_basis: Drugs Rules Rules 71 and 76; Revised Schedule M Part I 11.3.2

field: Schedule U particulars: analytical report (control) numbers for each raw material and for the product, actual production and packing quantities, and date of release for distribution or sale
why: Conditions of licence require batch manufacturing and test records with Schedule U particulars kept for five years; the eBMR should hold these explicitly (e.g., ARN per dispensed lot, release date).
legal_basis: Drugs Rules Rule 74 (and Rule 78) with Schedule U

field: Compression in-process check log at no more than 30-minute intervals, per-station start-of-run checks, and punch/die and sieve integrity checks before and after use
why: Part VIII fixes the maximum sampling interval and requires station-wise and before/after-use checks; the Tablets edition must carry these as mandatory structured fields.

field: Visual inspector eyesight-check validity and inspection-break records for 100% inspection of parenterals
why: Part II 10.8 and Part I 11.5.1 require regular eye checks and frequent breaks; the Injectables edition should capture inspector qualification status at sign-on.
legal_basis: Revised Schedule M Part II 10.8; Part I 11.5.1

clause: Part I, 2.3.3 (CAPA management) with PQS item (s) and 10.5-10.7 (follow-up)
url: https://egazette.gov.in (G.S.R. 922(E)); text checked in user-supplied copy, lines 750-757, 1087-1089, 567-568
requirement: Corrective and preventive actions must be completed promptly and effectively under documented procedures; there must be procedures for ongoing management and review of these actions, and their effectiveness must be verified during self-inspection. Investigations must go to an appropriate depth of root-cause analysis, identify the most likely root causes and monitor CAPA effectiveness; management evaluates self-inspection reports and corrective actions.
system_implications: CAPA records linked to deviations, OOS, complaints, PQR and self-inspection findings, with due dates, owners, effectiveness-check tasks and ageing reports; batch release should show open CAPAs relevant to the product/line (information, not necessarily a block).
verification_test: Create a CAPA from a deviation with an effectiveness check due in 90 days and confirm it appears in the overdue report after the due date; confirm the self-inspection module can list CAPAs whose effectiveness has not been verified.
note: confirmed in official text

clause: Part II, 4.11 and 4.11.1-4.11.2 (grade required per operation) and 1.1-1.3
requirement: Sterile operations are split into terminally sterilised and aseptic categories, and component preparation, product preparation, filling and sterilisation must be done in separate areas of appropriate grade. Terminally sterilised: filling generally at least Grade C; Grade A with at least C background where the product is at unusual environmental risk (slow filling, wide-necked or long-open containers); solutions and components prepared at least in D, or C if at unusual microbial risk; ointments, creams, suspensions and emulsions prepared and filled in C before terminal sterilisation. Aseptic: washed components handled in at least D; sterile materials not later sterilised or filtered handled in A with B background; solutions to be sterile-filtered prepared in C (D if closed); aseptic handling and filling, and exposed sterile equipment, in A with B background; partially stoppered lyophilisation containers moved in A/B or in sealed trays in B; exposed sterile semi-solids and suspensions not later filtered made in A/B.
system_implications: Each Injectables MBR step type carries a required minimum grade (and background grade) derived from process type (terminal vs aseptic) and product risk flags; the MBR validator refuses a step mapped to a room of lower grade; execution checks the room's current status and EM state.
verification_test: Map an aseptic filling step to a Grade C room in the MBR designer and confirm validation fails; for a terminally sterilised product flagged 'wide-neck container', confirm filling requires Grade A with at least Grade C background.
note: confirmed in official text (WHO 2011 / pre-2022 EU Annex 1 structure; EU 2022 has similar grade expectations with a contamination control strategy overlay).

clause: Part I, 14.29-14.31 (finished-product quarantine, release, rejected materials) and Part VIII 6.2
url: https://egazette.gov.in (G.S.R. 922(E)); text checked in user-supplied copy, lines 1179-1180, 2121-2123, 2162-2163, 5742
requirement: Finished products stay in quarantine until final release and are then stored as usable stock under the manufacturer's conditions; the evaluation and documents needed for release are those of section 19. Rejected materials and products are clearly marked, stored separately in restricted areas and returned, reprocessed or destroyed promptly, with the action approved by authorised personnel and recorded. Printed tablets and capsules need QC approval before release for packaging or sale.
system_implications: Status model for bulk and finished goods (quarantine, released, rejected, on hold) owned by the eBMR/QMS with e-signed status changes; warehouse/ERP interfaces must honour the status; rejected lots require a recorded disposition approved by an authorised role.
verification_test: Complete packaging and confirm finished goods are created in 'quarantine' and cannot be shipped via the ERP interface until the release signature; reject a batch and confirm a disposition (destroy/reprocess/return) with approval is required to close it.
note: confirmed in official text

clause: Part VIII, 1.1, 1.6-1.10, 3.1-3.2 (dust control, cubicles, pressure cascade, mix-up prevention at compression)
url: https://egazette.gov.in (G.S.R. 922(E)); text checked in user-supplied copy, lines 5521-5524, 5703-5720, 5578-5583
requirement: Dry-product processing needs special dust and cross-contamination control, with enclosed dust-control systems where required. Each tablet press needs effective dust control and must sit in its own cubicle unless the same product runs on each machine or the press provides its own enclosed controlled environment; physical, procedural and labelling measures must prevent mix-ups of materials, granules and tablets at compression. Equipment must be checked so that no material lodges undetected, nozzles stay clean and lubricants do not leak into product. In a multi-product OSD site, dust must not move between cubicles; the corridor is kept at a higher pressure than cubicles and cubicles above atmospheric, while highly potent products run under a negative pressure cascade.
system_implications: Room master data for OSD cubicles (pressure regime, dedicated/segregated flags, potent-product negative-pressure rooms); compression step requires identity labels on hoppers, containers and machine, verified by scan; equipment status includes 'lubricant leak check' and nozzle cleanliness in pre-use checks.
verification_test: Attempt to load granules from a container labelled for another batch into a press (scan mismatch) and confirm refusal; schedule a highly potent product in a positive-pressure cubicle and confirm it is blocked.
note: confirmed in official text

field: Marketer name and address (where different from the manufacturer) and reference to the marketer-manufacturer agreement
why: Marketers who sell drugs made by another manufacturer share responsibility for quality and must have a written agreement; labels must show the marketer, and the eBPR/artwork must carry both manufacturer (with licence number) and marketer details for India packs.
legal_basis: Drugs Rules Rules 84D and 84E (marketer agreement and responsibility, inserted by the 2020 amendment) and Rule 96(1)(xiii)

requirement: Where Indian rules and FDA/EU rules differ, a batch made for several markets must satisfy the strictest applicable rule. Known differences to encode: batch-record retention (India: longest of expiry+1y under Schedule M and 5 years under Rule 74, or expiry+2y for Rule 78 test records; FDA expiry+1y; EU longest of expiry+1y and certification+5y); retained/reference samples (India expiry+3 months under the Drugs Rules; FDA and EU expiry+1y); media-fill acceptance (India and FDA allow limited contaminated units with investigation; EU 2022 treats any growth as failure); Grade A viable limit (India '<1' average; EU 'no growth'); clean-room particle tables (India/WHO 2011 values vs EU 2022 values); HEPA leak-test interval (India 6-12 months); compression IPC interval (India at most 30 minutes; FDA/EU firm-defined); annual self-inspection (India only); new batch number for reworked batches (India/WHO only); hold time in MFR/BPR, date of manufacture on label, MRP and Schedule H/H1/X panels (India only); non-API excipient release without testing (allowed in India, not for FDA/EU identity testing); pharmacopoeial limits (IP vs USP vs Ph. Eur.).
system_implications: Implement a versioned, market-keyed rule table consulted at MBR approval, batch execution, release and archiving; each batch carries its target markets (India domestic, export-only country list), and the engine resolves every parameter to the strictest value, logging which market drove the result.
verification_test: Create one product with markets {India} and another with {India, EU, US}; confirm the second resolves to: retention max(expiry+1y, mfg+5y, cert+5y), sample retention expiry+1y, APS any-growth-fails, Grade A viable no-growth, 30-minute compression IPC, annual self-inspection flag, new batch number on rework, and mandatory identity test for excipients; confirm the rule-resolution log names the governing market for each.
